claim: A GGGGCC (G4C2) hexanucleotide repeat expansion (HRE) in chromosome nine open reading frame 72 (C9orf72) is the most common genetic cause of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD), accounting for up to 40% of cases of familial ALS.
source: A GGGGCC (G4C2) hexanucleotide repeat expansion (HRE) in chromosome nine open reading frame 72 (C9orf72) is the most common genetic cause of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD), accounting for up to 40% of cases of familial ALS (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; ITALSGEN Consortium et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011 and ITALSGEN Consortium et al., 2011

claim: ALS and/or FTD caused by mutations in C9orf72 (C9-ALS/FTD) is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.
source: ALS and/or FTD caused by mutations in C9orf72 (C9-ALS/FTD) is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, suggesting that the HRE causes disease through gain-of-function or haploinsufficiency (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; Ling et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011 and Ling et al., 2013

claim: The autosomal dominant inheritance pattern suggests that the HRE causes disease through gain-of-function or haploinsufficiency.
source: ALS and/or FTD caused by mutations in C9orf72 (C9-ALS/FTD) is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, suggesting that the HRE causes disease through gain-of-function or haploinsufficiency (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; Ling et al., 2013).
evidence: Inference based on inheritance pattern, supported by citations

claim: Loss of C9orf72 function has been linked to disruption of autophagy and lysosome function.
source: Loss of C9orf72 function has been linked to disruption of autophagy and lysosome function, though neurodegeneration is not observed in C9orf72 knockout mice (Liu et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2018; Webster et al., 2016), suggesting that C9-ALS/FTD is primarily caused by toxicity of the HRE.
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2018; Webster et al., 2016

claim: Neurodegeneration is not observed in C9orf72 knockout mice.
source: Loss of C9orf72 function has been linked to disruption of autophagy and lysosome function, though neurodegeneration is not observed in C9orf72 knockout mice (Liu et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2018; Webster et al., 2016), suggesting that C9-ALS/FTD is primarily caused by toxicity of the HRE.
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2018; Webster et al., 2016

claim: C9-ALS/FTD is primarily caused by toxicity of the HRE.
source: Loss of C9orf72 function has been linked to disruption of autophagy and lysosome function, though neurodegeneration is not observed in C9orf72 knockout mice (Liu et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2018; Webster et al., 2016), suggesting that C9-ALS/FTD is primarily caused by toxicity of the HRE.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that C9orf72 knockout mice do not show neurodegeneration, supported by citations

claim: Expression of G4C2 repeats causes neurotoxicity in Drosophila and cell culture models of C9-ALS.
source: Furthermore, expression of G4C2 repeats causes neurotoxicity in Drosophila and cell culture models of C9-ALS (Goodman et al., 2019a; Kramer et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goodman et al., 2019a; Kramer et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2015

claim: G4C2 repeat toxicity has been proposed to occur through either G4C2 repeat RNA-mediated sequestration of RNA-binding proteins or translation of the G4C2 repeats into dipeptide-repeat proteins (DPRs) through non-canonical repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation.
source: This toxicity has been proposed to occur through either G4C2 repeat RNA-mediated sequestration of RNA-binding proteins or translation of the G4C2 repeats into dipeptide-repeat proteins (DPRs) through non-canonical repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation (Donnelly et al., 2013; Goodman et al., 2019a; Mori et al., 2013; Tran et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Donnelly et al., 2013; Goodman et al., 2019a; Mori et al., 2013; Tran et al., 2015

claim: Modulation of the nucleocytoplasmic transport (NCT) pathway is a potent modifier of G4C2 toxicity in both fly and iPS neuron models of C9-ALS.
source: We previously conducted a Drosophila screen of candidate proteins that bound with moderate-to-high affinity to G4C2 RNA and identified modulation of the nucleocytoplasmic transport (NCT) pathway as a potent modifier of G4C2 toxicity in both fly and iPS neuron models of C9-ALS (Zhang et al., 2015a), a finding that has also been made by other groups (Freibaum et al., 2015; Jovičić et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2015a; Freibaum et al., 2015; Jovičić et al., 2015

claim: Potential mechanisms for G4C2 HRE disruption of NCT include G4C2 RNA binding to the master NCT regulator RanGAP.
source: The mechanisms by which the G4C2 HRE disrupts NCT remain unclear, but potential mechanisms include G4C2 RNA binding to the master NCT regulator RanGAP (Zhang et al., 2015a), DPRs disrupting the nuclear pore complex (Boeynaems et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2016), stress granules sequestering NCT factors (Zhang et al., 2018), or cytoplasmic TDP-43-dependent dysregulation of karyopherin-α (Chou et al., 2018; Gasset-Rosa et al., 2019; Solomon et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2015a

claim: Potential mechanisms for G4C2 HRE disruption of NCT include DPRs disrupting the nuclear pore complex.
source: The mechanisms by which the G4C2 HRE disrupts NCT remain unclear, but potential mechanisms include G4C2 RNA binding to the master NCT regulator RanGAP (Zhang et al., 2015a), DPRs disrupting the nuclear pore complex (Boeynaems et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2016), stress granules sequestering NCT factors (Zhang et al., 2018), or cytoplasmic TDP-43-dependent dysregulation of karyopherin-α (Chou et al., 2018; Gasset-Rosa et al., 2019; Solomon et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boeynaems et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2016

claim: Potential mechanisms for G4C2 HRE disruption of NCT include stress granules sequestering NCT factors.
source: The mechanisms by which the G4C2 HRE disrupts NCT remain unclear, but potential mechanisms include G4C2 RNA binding to the master NCT regulator RanGAP (Zhang et al., 2015a), DPRs disrupting the nuclear pore complex (Boeynaems et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2016), stress granules sequestering NCT factors (Zhang et al., 2018), or cytoplasmic TDP-43-dependent dysregulation of karyopherin-α (Chou et al., 2018; Gasset-Rosa et al., 2019; Solomon et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018

claim: Potential mechanisms for G4C2 HRE disruption of NCT include cytoplasmic TDP-43-dependent dysregulation of karyopherin-α.
source: The mechanisms by which the G4C2 HRE disrupts NCT remain unclear, but potential mechanisms include G4C2 RNA binding to the master NCT regulator RanGAP (Zhang et al., 2015a), DPRs disrupting the nuclear pore complex (Boeynaems et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2016), stress granules sequestering NCT factors (Zhang et al., 2018), or cytoplasmic TDP-43-dependent dysregulation of karyopherin-α (Chou et al., 2018; Gasset-Rosa et al., 2019; Solomon et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chou et al., 2018; Gasset-Rosa et al., 2019; Solomon et al., 2018

claim: NCT disruption may be a common mechanism in several neurodegenerative diseases including Huntington's disease and Alzheimer's disease.
source: Recently, a role for NCT disruption in Huntington's disease and Alzheimer's disease has been proposed, indicating that NCT disruption may be a common mechanism in several neurodegenerative diseases (Eftekharzadeh et al., 2018; Gasset-Rosa et al., 2017; Grima et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eftekharzadeh et al., 2018; Gasset-Rosa et al., 2017; Grima et al., 2017

claim: ref(2)P, the Drosophila homolog of p62/SQSTM1, was identified as a modifier of G4C2-mediated neurodegeneration in a Drosophila screen.
source: In a Drosophila screen for modifiers of G4C2-mediated neurodegeneration (Zhang et al., 2015a), we identified refractory to sigma P (ref(2)P), the Drosophila homolog of p62/SQSTM1 (Sequestosome 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2015a

claim: p62/SQSTM1 functions in macroautophagy.
source: p62/SQSTM1 functions in macroautophagy (hereafter termed autophagy), and mutations in p62/SQSTM1 are a rare genetic cause of ALS/FTD (Cirulli et al., 2015; Le Ber et al., 2013; Teyssou et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge and citations

claim: Mutations in p62/SQSTM1 are a rare genetic cause of ALS/FTD.
source: p62/SQSTM1 functions in macroautophagy (hereafter termed autophagy), and mutations in p62/SQSTM1 are a rare genetic cause of ALS/FTD (Cirulli et al., 2015; Le Ber et al., 2013; Teyssou et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cirulli et al., 2015; Le Ber et al., 2013; Teyssou et al., 2013

claim: Many genes implicated in ALS/FTD function in autophagy.
source: Interestingly, many other genes implicated in ALS/FTD function in autophagy (Evans and Holzbaur, 2019; Lin et al., 2017; Ramesh and Pandey, 2017) such as tank-binding kinase 1 (TBK1), optineurin (OPTN1), ubiquilin 2 and 4 (UBQLN2 and 4), valosin-containing protein (VCP), charged multivesicular body protein 2B (CHMP2B), VAMP-associated protein B (VapB), and the C9orf72 protein itself (O'Rourke et al., 2015; Sellier et al., 2016; Sullivan et al., 2016; Ugolino et al., 2016; Webster et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Evans and Holzbaur, 2019; Lin et al., 2017; Ramesh and Pandey, 2017 and additional citations for specific genes

claim: Deletion of key autophagy genes in neurons is sufficient to cause neurodegeneration in mice.
source: Deletion of key autophagy genes in neurons is sufficient to cause neurodegeneration in mice (Hara et al., 2006; Komatsu et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hara et al., 2006; Komatsu et al., 2006

claim: Expression of 30 G4C2 repeats (30R) in the eye using GMR-Gal4 results in progressive photoreceptor degeneration and visible ommatidial disruption by day 15.
source: Expression of 30 G4C2 repeats (30R) in the eye using GMR-Gal4 results in progressive photoreceptor degeneration and visible ommatidial disruption by day 15 (Figure 1A; Xu et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2015a).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1A and citations to Xu et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2015a

claim: UAS-ref(2)PRNAi was among the strongest of 32 suppressors of G4C2-mediated eye degeneration in a genetic modifier screen.
source: In a genetic modifier screen of over 800 RNAi lines, UAS-ref(2)PRNAi was among the strongest of 32 suppressors of G4C2-mediated eye degeneration (Zhang et al., 2015a; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2015a and Figure 1A

claim: Knockdown of ref(2)P suppresses eye degeneration caused by G4C2 repeats.
source: Knockdown of ref(2)P suppresses eye degeneration, whereas overexpression of ref(2)P enhances this phenotype (Figure 1A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A-B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Overexpression of ref(2)P enhances eye degeneration caused by G4C2 repeats.
source: Knockdown of ref(2)P suppresses eye degeneration, whereas overexpression of ref(2)P enhances this phenotype (Figure 1A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A-B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: ref(2)P RNAi #1 expression reduced ref(2)P mRNA levels by ~80%.
source: ref(2)P RNAi #1 expression reduced ref(2)P mRNA levels by ~80%, but did not alter G4C2 RNA levels in 30R expressing eyes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C), suggesting that ref(2)P acts downstream of G4C2 transcription.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C

claim: ref(2)P RNAi did not alter G4C2 RNA levels in 30R expressing eyes.
source: ref(2)P RNAi #1 expression reduced ref(2)P mRNA levels by ~80%, but did not alter G4C2 RNA levels in 30R expressing eyes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C), suggesting that ref(2)P acts downstream of G4C2 transcription.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C

claim: ref(2)P acts downstream of G4C2 transcription.
source: ref(2)P RNAi #1 expression reduced ref(2)P mRNA levels by ~80%, but did not alter G4C2 RNA levels in 30R expressing eyes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C), suggesting that ref(2)P acts downstream of G4C2 transcription.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that ref(2)P knockdown does not alter G4C2 RNA levels

claim: Knockdown of ref(2)P rescues eye degeneration in a G4C2 model expressing 36 G4C2 repeats (36R).
source: Similarly, knockdown of ref(2)P also rescued eye degeneration in a second G4C2 model expressing 36 G4C2 repeats (36R) (Mizielinska et al., 2014; Figure 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C-D and citation to Mizielinska et al., 2014

claim: Expression of 30R or 44R in motor neurons with vGlut-Gal4 leads to paralysis and lethality during pupal development.
source: As shown in Figure 1E–F, while expression of either 30R or 44R in motor neurons with vGlut-Gal4 leads to paralysis and lethality during pupal development, knockdown of ref(2)P partially rescues this phenotype, whereas overexpression of ref(2)P enhances the pupal lethality observed with 44R expression.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1E-F

claim: Knockdown of ref(2)P partially rescues paralysis and lethality during pupal development caused by 30R or 44R expression in motor neurons.
source: As shown in Figure 1E–F, while expression of either 30R or 44R in motor neurons with vGlut-Gal4 leads to paralysis and lethality during pupal development, knockdown of ref(2)P partially rescues this phenotype, whereas overexpression of ref(2)P enhances the pupal lethality observed with 44R expression.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1E-F

claim: Overexpression of ref(2)P enhances the pupal lethality observed with 44R expression.
source: As shown in Figure 1E–F, while expression of either 30R or 44R in motor neurons with vGlut-Gal4 leads to paralysis and lethality during pupal development, knockdown of ref(2)P partially rescues this phenotype, whereas overexpression of ref(2)P enhances the pupal lethality observed with 44R expression.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1E-F

claim: ref(2)P is required for G4C2-mediated toxicity during Drosophila development.
source: These data suggest that ref(2)P is required for G4C2-mediated toxicity during Drosophila development.
evidence: Inference based on the rescue of developmental lethality by ref(2)P knockdown

claim: ref(2)P knockdown suppresses age-dependent neurodegeneration caused by 30R expression.
source: To determine whether ref(2)P knockdown is able to suppress age-dependent neurodegeneration, we used a pan-neuronal, inducible 'GeneSwitch' driver (elavGS) in which 30R-expression leads to a marked reduction in climbing ability after 7 days (Figure 1G). This climbing defect is suppressed with coexpression of ref(2)P RNAi, suggesting that ref(2)P contributes to G4C2-mediated neurotoxicity in the adult nervous system.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1G

claim: 30R-expression leads to a marked reduction in climbing ability after 7 days in adult flies.
source: To determine whether ref(2)P knockdown is able to suppress age-dependent neurodegeneration, we used a pan-neuronal, inducible 'GeneSwitch' driver (elavGS) in which 30R-expression leads to a marked reduction in climbing ability after 7 days (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1G

claim: ref(2)P contributes to G4C2-mediated neurotoxicity in the adult nervous system.
source: This climbing defect is suppressed with coexpression of ref(2)P RNAi, suggesting that ref(2)P contributes to G4C2-mediated neurotoxicity in the adult nervous system.
evidence: Inference based on the rescue of climbing defect by ref(2)P knockdown

claim: ref(2)P RNAi partially rescues poly(GR)36-mediated eye degeneration.
source: Since RAN-translation of arginine-containing DPRs have been implicated in G4C2-mediated toxicity in Drosophila (Kwon et al., 2014; Mizielinska et al., 2014), we next tested whether ref(2)P knockdown rescues poly-glycine-arginine (GR) repeat-mediated toxicity. As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, ref(2)P RNAi partially rescues the severe eye degeneration phenotype caused by poly(GR)36 expression.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and citations to Kwon et al., 2014; Mizielinska et al., 2014

claim: p62/SQSTM1-positive inclusions are a common pathologic feature seen in brains of C9-ALS/FTD patients where they colocalize with ubiquitin and DPRs.
source: p62/SQSTM1-positive inclusions are a common pathologic feature seen in brains of C9-ALS/FTD patients where they colocalize with ubiquitin and DPRs (Al-Sarraj et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Al-Sarraj et al., 2011

claim: Expression of 30R leads to the formation of many large p62:GFP puncta in motor neuron cell bodies that strongly colocalize with poly-ubiquitinated proteins.
source: Expression of 30R leads to the formation of many large p62:GFP puncta in cell bodies compared to controls that strongly colocalize with poly-ubiquitinated proteins (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A-B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B

claim: p62 and poly-ubiquitin are strongly upregulated in flies ubiquitously expressing 30R.
source: Western blot analysis demonstrates that p62 and poly-ubiquitin are strongly upregulated in flies ubiquitously expressing 30R (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-D

claim: Endogenous p62 accumulations colocalize with polyubiquitinated proteins in the ventral nerve cord and salivary gland of flies ubiquitously overexpressing 30R.
source: Similarly, immunofluorescence staining with a p62 antibody shows endogenous p62 accumulations colocalizing with polyubiquitinated proteins in the ventral nerve cord and salivary gland of flies ubiquitously overexpressing 30R (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E

claim: G4C2 repeat expression in fly models recapitulates the p62 accumulation with ubiquitinated protein aggregates seen in C9-ALS/FTD patient tissue and iPS neurons.
source: These data show that G4C2 repeat expression in fly models recapitulates the p62 accumulation with ubiquitinated protein aggregates seen in C9-ALS/FTD patient tissue and iPS neurons (Almeida et al., 2013; Mackenzie et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Almeida et al., 2013; Mackenzie et al., 2014

claim: ref(2)P transcript levels are unchanged in G4C2 repeat-expressing larvae.
source: Using qRT-PCR, we find that ref(2)P transcript levels are unchanged in G4C2 repeat-expressing larvae (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that G4C2 repeats cause p62 upregulation by inhibiting p62 degradation.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F

claim: G4C2 repeats cause p62 upregulation by inhibiting p62 degradation.
source: Using qRT-PCR, we find that ref(2)P transcript levels are unchanged in G4C2 repeat-expressing larvae (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that G4C2 repeats cause p62 upregulation by inhibiting p62 degradation.
evidence: Inference based on unchanged transcript levels but increased protein levels

claim: p62:GFP accumulation and loss of mCherry:Atg8 puncta were recapitulated in 36R and poly(GR)36 Drosophila models of C9-ALS/FTD.
source: p62:GFP accumulation and loss of mCherry:Atg8 puncta were recapitulated in 36R and poly(GR)36 Drosophila models of C9-ALS/FTD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–J).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G-J

claim: Reduction of mCherry:Atg8-positive vesicles coupled with the accumulation of p62 and ubiquitin suggest that autophagic flux is impaired in fly models of C9-ALS/FTD.
source: Reduction of mCherry:Atg8-positive vesicles coupled with the accumulation of p62 and ubiquitin suggest that autophagic flux is impaired in these fly models of C9-ALS/FTD.
evidence: Inference based on multiple autophagy markers

claim: The accumulation of GFP:Lamp-positive vesicles in 30R-expressing motor neurons suggests a defect in lysosomal acidity or targeting of GFP:Lamp to mature lysosomes.
source: Since GFP is largely quenched by the acidity of lysosomes in control animals (Pulipparacharuvil et al., 2005), the accumulation of GFP:Lamp-positive vesicles in 30R-expressing motor neurons suggests a defect in lysosomal acidity or targeting of GFP:Lamp to mature lysosomes (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: Inference based on GFP quenching properties and data shown in Figure 2G-H, supported by citation to Pulipparacharuvil et al., 2005

claim: There is a marked increase in size and number of late endosomes and lysosomes using genomically tagged Rab7:YFP throughout 30R-expressing motor neurons.
source: Furthermore, we observe a marked increase in size and number of late endosomes and lysosomes using genomically tagged Ras-related GTP-binding protein 7, Rab7:YFP, throughout 30R-expressing motor neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) without alterations in early endosomes labeled with Rab5:YFP (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claim: There are no alterations in early endosomes labeled with Rab5:YFP in 30R-expressing motor neurons.
source: Furthermore, we observe a marked increase in size and number of late endosomes and lysosomes using genomically tagged Ras-related GTP-binding protein 7, Rab7:YFP, throughout 30R-expressing motor neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) without alterations in early endosomes labeled with Rab5:YFP (data not shown).
evidence: Stated in text but data not shown

claim: There is a marked expansion of the late endosome/lysosome compartment in G4C2-expressing neurons.
source: Together, these data demonstrate a marked expansion of the late endosome/lysosome compartment in G4C2-expressing neurons.
evidence: Inference based on multiple lysosomal markers

claim: There is no decrease in mCherry:Atg8+, Rab7:GFP+ amphisomes in G4C2-expressing motor neuron cell bodies.
source: Though accumulation of p62 and ubiquitinated proteins could be caused by a failure of autophagic vesicles to fuse with the degradative endolysosomal compartment, we did not detect a decrease in mCherry:Atg8+, Rab7:GFP+ amphisomes in G4C2-expressing motor neuron cell bodies (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B-F

claim: Free lysosomal GFP is not observed in G4C2-expressing larvae, suggesting an impairment in GFP:mCherry:Atg8 degradation by the lysosome.
source: To assess autophagolysosomal function after fusion, we performed a GFP liberation assay on larvae expressing GFP:mCherry:Atg8 (Klionsky et al., 2016; Mauvezin et al., 2014). GFP is degraded more slowly than the rest of the mCherry:Atg8 protein, leaving a population of free GFP in functioning lysosomes. Free lysosomal GFP is not observed in G4C2-expressing larvae, suggesting an impairment in GFP:mCherry:Atg8 degradation by the lysosome (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2F and citations to Klionsky et al., 2016; Mauvezin et al., 2014

claim: Larvae ubiquitously expressing 30R show an increase in the ratio of pro-Cp1 to Cp1, indicating a decrease in pro-Cp1 cleavage efficiency.
source: To directly probe lysosome enzymatic activity, we performed Western analysis of Drosophila cathepsin Cp1. Whereas pro-Cp1 is normally cleaved to its mature form by acid hydrolases in lysosomes (Kinser and Dolph, 2012), larvae ubiquitously expressing 30R show an increase in the ratio of pro-Cp1 to Cp1, indicating a decrease in pro-Cp1 cleavage efficiency (Figure 2I–J).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2I-J and citation to Kinser and Dolph, 2012

claim: Lysosomes are expanded and dysfunctional in G4C2 repeat-expressing animals.
source: Together, these data suggest that lysosomes are expanded and dysfunctional in G4C2 repeat-expressing animals.
evidence: Inference based on multiple lysosomal assays

claim: Rh1 >30R photoreceptors show only a mild reduction of ON transient amplitude at 28 days, but a complete loss of ON and OFF transients and a decrease in ERG amplitude by 56 days.
source: Rh1 >30R PRs show only a mild reduction of ON transient amplitude at 28 days, but a complete loss of ON and OFF transients and a decrease in ERG amplitude by 56 days (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D), indicating a slow and progressive loss of synaptic transmission and impaired phototransduction respectively.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D

claim: There is a marked loss of photoreceptors and synaptic terminals by 54 days which are not observed at 28 days in Rh1 >30R flies.
source: These changes also correspond to a marked loss of photoreceptors and synaptic terminals by 54 days which are not observed at 28 days (Figure 3A–B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A-B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E

claim: There is a marked increase in the size and number of multilamellar bodies (MLBs) at 28 days in 30R-expressing photoreceptor neurons.
source: We therefore examined autophagic structures by TEM at 28 days, prior to cell loss. Strikingly, we observe a marked increase in the size and number of multilamellar bodies (MLBs) (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C-D

claim: MLBs are commonly observed in lysosomal storage diseases and result from a deficiency of lysosomal hydrolases and accumulations of lysosomal lipids and membranes.
source: MLBs are commonly observed in lysosomal storage diseases and result from a deficiency of lysosomal hydrolases and accumulations of lysosomal lipids and membranes (Hariri et al., 2000; Weaver et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hariri et al., 2000; Weaver et al., 2002

claim: There is a significant increase in the number of autolysosomes in 30R-expressing photoreceptor neurons at 28 days.
source: Though we did not detect an alteration in the number of autophagosomes, lysosomes, or multivesicular bodies, we did see a significant increase in the number of autolysosomes (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C-D

claim: Autophagolysosomal function is disrupted in G4C2-expressing photoreceptor neurons at early stages of degeneration.
source: These data suggest that autophagolysosomal function is disrupted in G4C2-expressing photoreceptor neurons at early stages of degeneration.
evidence: Inference based on TEM data showing MLB accumulation before cell loss

claim: Activation of early steps in the autophagic pathway (e.g. by Atg1 overexpression) suppresses eye degeneration.
source: Indeed, in a candidate-based screen, activation of early steps in the autophagic pathway (e.g. by Atg1 overexpression) suppresses eye degeneration and blocking autophagosome/lysosome fusion (e.g. by Snap29 knockdown) enhances eye degeneration (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 1

claim: Blocking autophagosome/lysosome fusion (e.g. by Snap29 knockdown) enhances eye degeneration.
source: Indeed, in a candidate-based screen, activation of early steps in the autophagic pathway (e.g. by Atg1 overexpression) suppresses eye degeneration and blocking autophagosome/lysosome fusion (e.g. by Snap29 knockdown) enhances eye degeneration (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 1

claim: Pharmacologic activation of autophagy via inhibition of mTor with rapamycin rescues neurodegenerative phenotypes and p62 accumulation.
source: Similarly, pharmacologic activation of autophagy via inhibition of mTor with rapamycin or mTor-independent activation via trehalose (Sarkar et al., 2007) rescues neurodegenerative phenotypes and p62 accumulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G–K).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G-K and citation to Sarkar et al., 2007

claim: mTor-independent activation of autophagy via trehalose rescues neurodegenerative phenotypes and p62 accumulation.
source: Similarly, pharmacologic activation of autophagy via inhibition of mTor with rapamycin or mTor-independent activation via trehalose (Sarkar et al., 2007) rescues neurodegenerative phenotypes and p62 accumulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G–K).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G-K and citation to Sarkar et al., 2007

claim: Promoting autophagy or lysosomal fusion are potent suppressors of G4C2-mediated neurodegeneration.
source: Together, these data show that promoting autophagy or lysosomal fusion are potent suppressors of G4C2-mediated neurodegeneration.
evidence: Inference based on genetic and pharmacological rescue experiments

claim: Knockdown of ref(2)P does not restore nuclear localization of S-GFP in G4C2 repeat-expressing cells.
source: We first tested whether knockdown of ref(2)P rescues the mislocalization of the NCT reporter shuttle-GFP (S-GFP) containing both a nuclear localization sequence (NLS) and nuclear export sequence (NES). G4C2 repeat expression causes mislocalization of S-GFP to the cytoplasm (Zhang et al., 2015a), but knockdown of ref(2)P does not restore nuclear localization (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and citation to Zhang et al., 2015a

claim: Stimulation of autophagy with rapamycin or trehalose fails to rescue S-GFP mislocalization in G4C2 expressing salivary glands.
source: Similarly, stimulation of autophagy with rapamycin or trehalose fails to rescue S-GFP mislocalization in G4C2 expressing salivary glands (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Autophagy defects are either independent of or downstream of NCT defects.
source: Stimulating autophagy does not rescue NCT defects although it can rescue neurodegeneration, suggesting that autophagy defects are either independent of or downstream of NCT defects.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that autophagy stimulation rescues neurodegeneration but not NCT defects

claim: RanGAP knockdown increases the number and size of p62:GFP puncta, similar to the effects of overexpressing the G4C2 repeats.
source: Indeed, RanGAP knockdown increases the number and size of p62:GFP puncta, similar to the effects of overexpressing the G4C2 repeats (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that NCT disruption is sufficient to disrupt autophagic flux in Drosophila motor neurons.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: NCT disruption is sufficient to disrupt autophagic flux in Drosophila motor neurons.
